title: OK as an editor, clumsy file manager
body: This app has no MDI paradigm — no open file list, tabs, etc. So your workflow is expected to be “one file at a time”. What’s worse, you can’t get a list of edited files — you have to, one-by-one, “upload” them to your remote server or Dropbox. There’s not even a classic “*filename” indicator that a file has been changed. So keeping your files in sync is pretty much down to remembering what you’ve changed. So this editor works fine for a one-off update to a single property in a single file, but its poor file management makes it a bad choice for a code IDE.

title: The Dream of a Subscription Text Editor
body: Coming from the days where one purchased applications, and purchased subsequent updates outright, always have I longed for a subscription text editor. One that I would purchase repeatedly, regardless of whether or not it had been upgraded, and regardless of whether or not those upgrades applied to me. Well, after many agonizing years, that dream is now a reality. If any application genre screamed out to be a subscription, it is the text editor, what with all of the streaming data they have to provide to the user on a monthly basis. Also, unlike the hordes of starving developers that came before them, these guys finally realized that they could produce a better product if only they could eat every day, while maintaining a roof over their head. This was clearly not possible under the previous scheme, where a product was paid for without further obligation by the customer a/k/a “The Dark Days of Reason”. Instead of laboring under these gulag-esque conditions, the developers of Textastic have finally corrected one of the most grievous injustices since World War Two: the ruthless exploitation of the mobile software developer by the greedy, irrational, demanding customers who constantly demand the the devs fix glaring bugs, while not paying one red scent extra for their fixing. Instead of paying more the buggier an app was, selfish consumers wanted to pay the same price for buggy apps that they paid for more stable apps. This is an abomination that Textastic had the integrity, nay, courage to rectify. In my humble opinion, they have created a dream that you too can live. Go ahead. Push that button in the upper-right corner. Only through your support, will this economic model survive, and relegate to the history books that most heinous of paradigms known as “ownership”. In the future, you will own nothing and be happy. You do not have to wait, though. The future is here today, if only you would click that button. Set yourself free. Do it now.

It also needs more variety when it comes to theming and code editor options. It’s local file system, albeit a symptom of the underpowered iOS, is a bit confusing and unintuitive. Lastly, the interface just has something about it that feels unpolished. Good work so far, but there is so much that this editor leaves you wanting.

Working Copy is a git client for iOS which integrates with Textastic - this combo does a good job at bringing the git workflow to your iPad. Reasons for not getting my last star: I would love to be able to beautify (aka format) my code; I would appreciate native GitHub integration with full control; and the ability to run front-end compilers/tooling such as npm, gulp, scss, and typescript. Oh and FWIW I'm running this on a 2nd gen iPad mini, primarily working with HTML/CSS/JS through Box, Google Drive, and Github.

My peeve is no shortcut to comment blocks, hard to believe that's been left undone for a really long time. But otherwise excellent. You can use it for C# and other non-Web technologies, but when you're doing something Web like HTML / JS / JQ / CSS, the ability to preview in Safari (with the eyeglasses icon) is very helpful. You can use './whatever.file' style to refer to localized CSS and script files so you don't have to be online either. Especially valuable if like me you have an independent i-device and you don't always have WiFi to get jQuery etc. from a CDN. Needs comment blocks, sad, and there are a few other minor gripes, but generally top-notch in all regards.

No monthly or subscription charges of any kind, and I can't express how amazing this is to use. Syncing across devices and platforms is flawless, you can FTP/SFTP or use whatever method you prefer to remotely download files and edit/upload them. If you're in the market for any text editor, do yourself a favor - end the search here and you'll see what I mean. You'll never look back, either. Did I mention how well-maintained and stable it is? Well there's more features than you may even need, but again, the price is beyond fair. I strongly urge people to see what you've been missing & you'll understand the first few minutes of use. Enjoy! --- Original Review: [~ 2014]: (5/5 star rating) Textastic is an app I've been using as my go-to text editor and code interface for web-development to basic markdown editing for years. It's the first app I use each time I copy a website's source text and paste into an editor to see what I'm looking for/at. I remember when I first bought this app years ago, it was SO perfectly made, I had mistaken it for one of Panic's applications, (see: Coda, Transmit, Prompt, etc.) If you have Textastic on your iPhone, iPod touch, or iPad - you essentially have a powerhouse text editor that is capable of performing the same tasks as Sublime Text, Text Wrangler, BBEdit, ByWord, and much, much more all rolled into one iOS app. (And if you're still not using Desktop's Textastic, I can't say what you're still doing with whatever text editor you currently use. I understand that Text Wrangler is free, but Textastic flat out curb stomps on any other OS X Text Editor, (save for Coda 2.5 - which is essentially a bulkier and more powerful app for website development that happens to have Textastic's capabilities integrated into it, but I purchased them both all the same.) GO GO GO.

title: Well worth the price
body: Intuitive actions, easy-to-identify formatting symbols, clean interface - This app has boosted my productivity tenfold by giving me a place to record those "aha" code moments (that's not the apple notes app).

title: Amazing as always
body: I write books. Long books. And I use Markdown to do it. This has been my go-to app on both Mac and iOS for writing for at least a year now. It handles large documents well and has all the features that makes writing these large documents easy (like highlighting all matching strings when using "Find" and displaying a list of all instances of that string; being able to jump to different sections/chapters/headers defined with the markdown syntax; etc.). In a word, is just good. It's just good. It's everything I'd expect from a professional plain text editor on a desktop OS but for iOS, and that's awesome.
